newsitem.title: NORWAY: Christiania 1996 profits burdened by costs.
newsitem.headline: Christiania 1996 profits burdened by costs.

text.p: Norway's second biggest commercial bank, Christiania Bank og Kreditkasse, said on Wednesday higher costs helped reduce 1996 net profits.
But net interest income, the bank's core business, and other income rose.
Net profits fell to 2.15 billion crowns ($319 million) from 2.78 billion, corresponding to earnings per share of 3.91 crowns, down from 5.04 crowns in 1995.

"I am most satisfied with the bank's income side," chief executive officer Borger Lenth said in a statement. "We have succeeded in increasing the net interest income despite the keen competition in the market. In addition we see that non-interest income...shows a rising trend."
Net interest income increased to 3.43 billion crowns from 3.30 billion while non-interest income, including commissions and fees, rose to 1.49 billion from 1.32 billion.
Non-interest expenses, however, increased to 3.37 million crowns from 2.94 billion mainly because of a restructuring charge of 228 million crowns.
"The charge of 228 million crowns...will be applied in making the bank more cost-efficient in the course of the next couple of years," Lenth said.

Profits also fell because of a sharp reduction in the recovery of loans previously written off. Net writebacks, which have helped to sweeten the balance sheet in the past few years, shrank to 575 million crowns from 1.09 billion crowns in 1995.
Analyst expect the writebacks to gradually cease as old non-performing loans will decrease.
In the course of the year, total non-performing commitments were reduced by 0.8 billion crowns to 2.9 billion.
Losses on loans and guarantees where no specific loss allowance has been made amounted to 178 million crowns, down from 268 million in 1995.
"These losses are particularly low, and the bank will normally have losses on loans and guarantees larger than what has been experienced in the last three years," Christiania said in a statement.
Because of the booming Norwegian economy, the period of losses below normal was likely to continue for longer than assumed, it said.
"In light of this, the Board of Directors has deemed it justifiable to reduce the general loan loss allowance by 400 million crowns," Christiania said.

Norwegian banks returned to profits about two years ago after being mired in a financial crisis around 1990. Top banks were bailed out of the crisis by the government, which still keeps a controlling stake in Christiania and Den norske Bank (DnB) ) as a result of the rescue action.
